title: I used AI to turn a 20 year old idea into a hobby online game project
author: Matthias87
selftext:
I started playing Tibia in 2003. For years I wanted to run and develop my own server, but the honest problem was that I never had enough technical knowledge to maintain something of that size properly.

AI changed that for me.

About the last few months I have been building **Sentibia**, an OpenTibia project based around the classic 8.60 era. What surprised me is that the most useful part of AI was not actually “generate this function for me”.

It was being able to deal with the size of the project.

The server contains years of legacy C++, Lua, XML, database structures, maps, NPC scripts and quest logic. One of the biggest jobs, for example, was auditing the quest system. Instead of manually opening hundreds of scripts and trying to remember which storage connects to which NPC, monster or action, I could use AI agents to trace those relationships across the repository, create an audit, and then work through the broken or incomplete quest families one batch at a time.

That changed my role quite a bit.

Instead of trying to remember every implementation detail myself, I spend much more time defining how a system should behave, reviewing what was changed, testing it and deciding whether it actually belongs in the game.

I also ended up building things I originally had absolutely no intention of building.

There is now a separate web portal, a browser client, an Android client in development and an Operations Center for monitoring and controlling the server.

One of the more interesting examples was debugging a serious memory problem. The obvious symptom was the server process eventually getting killed. Following the code paths with AI-assisted analysis eventually exposed repeated NPC scans happening roughly twenty times per second. The fix wasn't particularly glamorous — caching, shared scanning and backoff — but finding the interaction across the codebase would have been extremely difficult for me a few years ago.

I still don't just accept generated code.

A lot of the development process has actually become:

**define behaviour → let the agent investigate/implement → run automated tests → inspect the result → test it myself → reject or refine it → merge**

And AI definitely makes mistakes. It can misunderstand legacy behaviour, “fix” something that was intentional, confidently follow the wrong source of truth or make a change far broader than requested. I've learned that giving it explicit boundaries and good acceptance tests is far more important than writing a clever prompt.

That has probably been the biggest lesson for me.

AI hasn't removed the need to understand the project. If anything, once you can make changes much faster, **knowing what you actually want becomes more important**, because it's also possible to make a very large mess much faster.

What it *has* done is lower the technical barrier enough that I could finally build something I had wanted to build since I was a teenager.

Sentibia is now live, and I'm at the slightly terrifying stage where real people can actually play what I've been building.
